caption_hook: West Virginia's hills hold coal swamps, a canyon-cutting sandstone and a cave-riddled seabed.

layers.name: PITTSBURGH COAL
layers.what: Vast peat swamps once covered the northern part of the state. Buried and compressed, they became the Pittsburgh coal bed, one of the most heavily mined coal beds in America.
layers.bonus: West Virginia is still one of the two biggest coal-producing states in the U.S.

layers.name: NUTTALL SANDSTONE
layers.hook: The cliffs of the New River Gorge
layers.what: Rivers dumped sand and gravel across an ancient lowland. Hardened into thick, tough sandstone, it forms the cliffs that line the New River Gorge, prized by rock climbers.
layers.bonus: The New River Gorge Bridge crosses it, towering 876 ft above the river.

layers.name: GREENBRIER LIMESTONE
layers.hook: A warm sea turned to cave country
layers.what: A clear tropical sea once covered the area, and shells and coral built up thick beds of limestone. Rainwater has been dissolving it ever since, hollowing out caves and sinkholes.
layers.bonus: The Greenbrier Valley is full of caves, including Lost World Caverns near Lewisburg.

layers.name: TUSCARORA SANDSTONE
layers.hook: A knife-edge fin of white rock
layers.what: Beach sand piled up along an ancient shoreline and cemented into very hard, quartz-rich rock. Folded and tilted by mountain-building, it now juts skyward as a towering stone fin.
layers.bonus: Seneca Rocks rises roughly 900 ft above the North Fork River.

layers.name: HARPERS FORMATION
layers.what: Ancient seafloor mud and sand were baked and squeezed during mountain building into shiny, layered phyllite. This is the rock where the Shenandoah meets the Potomac.
layers.bonus: Jefferson Rock, with its famous view, sits on this layered stone.
